title: Extracting conformal data from Loschmidt echoes after critical quenches
authors: Aleix Bou-Comas, Stefano Carignano, Sergio Cerezo-Roquebrún, Esperanza Lopez, Luca Tagliacozzo
abstract: Conformal field theory provides universal predictions for Loschmidt amplitudes following quenches from product states to critical Hamiltonians. Building on this observation, we develop a route to extracting conformal data from real-time dynamics without preparing critical low-energy states. After analytic continuation, the Loschmidt amplitude is described by a boundary-CFT partition function on a strip, whose transverse transfer matrix encodes both the boundary operator spectrum and the central charge. Local space-time perturbations of the amplitude are governed by equilibrium correlation functions, and therefore provide access to critical exponents. In parallel, generalized temporal entropies exhibit scaling with time analogous to the equilibrium scaling of spatial entanglement entropy. We show that the low-lying boundary spectrum can be reconstructed from the system-size dependence of finite-chain Loschmidt echoes, whose damped oscillations encode differences of boundary scaling dimensions. Finally, we propose a finite-size scaling protocol that can extract these quantities from simulations or experiments on state-of-the-art quantum platforms.
summary: The paper develops a method to extract universal Conformal Field Theory data from real-time Loschmidt echoes following quantum quenches. By mapping the time evolution onto a boundary-CFT partition function, the authors show that ratios of spectral splittings encode fundamental CFT parameters like scaling dimensions and central charge. This provides a robust theoretical framework for analyzing out-of-equilibrium dynamics in critical systems.
main_problem: The goal is to develop a method to extract universal Conformal Field Theory (CFT) data from real-time quantum dynamics, specifically using Loschmidt echoes after critical quenches, without needing to prepare the difficult-to-access critical low-energy states.
main_result: Ratios of spectral splittings derived from finite-size dependence of Loschmidt echoes are shown to be universal and directly encode differences in boundary scaling dimensions ($\Delta_i - \Delta_j$), allowing for a practical extraction protocol.
method: The analysis involves mapping the time evolution to a boundary-CFT partition function on a strip geometry, utilizing transverse transfer matrices whose spectra yield CFT data. Finite-size scaling protocols are developed by analyzing ratios of decay rates.
model_or_system: The study focuses on one-dimensional quantum systems undergoing a quench from an initial product state $|\psi_0angle$ to a critical Hamiltonian $H$. The dynamics are diagnosed using the Loschmidt amplitude, $A(T) = \langle\psi_0| e^{-iHT} |\psi_0angle$, which is related to boundary-CFT partition functions.
key_observables: Loschmidt amplitude/echo ($L(T)$), transverse transfer matrix spectrum (eigenvalues $\lambda_i$), generalized temporal entropies, and ratios of dynamical exponents ($\Delta_{ii}/\Delta_{11}$).
important_parameters: System size dependence ($N_X$), quench time ($T$), central charge ($c$), and boundary scaling dimensions ($\xi$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on analytic continuation from imaginary time (Euclidean) to real time, and the extraction protocols assume that finite-size effects can be systematically removed through ratios.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the tensor network representation of the Loschmidt amplitude via transverse contraction. Plots show linear relationships between logarithms of observables versus scaled time/temperature, confirming power-law decays predicted by CFT theory (e.g., slope $-1/8$).
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the connection between Loschmidt echoes and boundary-CFT partition functions on a strip. It then details how spectral properties of the transverse transfer matrix encode universal data like central charge and scaling dimensions, culminating in proposing finite-size scaling protocols for experimental/simulation extraction.
why_interesting: This work provides powerful theoretical tools to probe non-equilibrium quantum dynamics using measurable quantities (echoes) that bypass the need for complex state preparation, making it highly relevant for characterizing critical points in physical systems.
